q-345569.name: Question 1
q-345569.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}| &  & | \\ {u}_{1} & ⋯ & {u}_{n} \\ | &  & |\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}| &  & | \\ {v}_{1} & ⋯ & {v}_{m} \\ | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $U$ and $V$ above. Let $X$ be a $n\times m$ standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $X,$ what is the fourth principal component of the data?
q-345569.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned}
$$

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that:

- $\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ$ is a diagonal $m\times m$ matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix $C$, and

- $V$ is a $m\times m$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$

Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data.
So, the fourth principal component is ${v}_{4}.$

Question 1
?

U=[||u1⋯un||],V=[||v1⋯vm||] Consider the matrices U and V above. Let X be a n×m standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that X=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of X, what is the fourth principal component of the data?

a
v4
b
u4
c
u4v1
d
X4,4
e
u4uT4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector v1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector v2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to X is

C=1n−1XTX=1n−1(UΣVT)T(UΣVT)=1n−1VΣT(UTU)ΣVT=V(1n−1ΣTΣ)VT,

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix C. Notice that:

  • 1n−1ΣTΣ is a diagonal m×m matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix C, and

  • V is a m×m matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C.

Therefore, the columns of V are the principal components of the data. So, the fourth principal component is v4.

q-345556.name: Question 2
q-345556.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{4}{5} & 0 & -\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & 0 & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $U$ and $V$ above. Let $X$ be a $2\times 3$ standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $X,$ what is the third principal component of the data?
q-345556.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>{\lambda }_{3}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- the $3$rd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to the $3$rd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}.$

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned}
$$

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that:

- $\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ$ is a diagonal $3\times 3$ matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix $C$, and

- $V$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$

Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data.
So, the third principal component is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

q-343711.name: Question 5
q-343711.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $U$ and $V$ above. Let $X$ be a $2\times 3$ standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $X,$ what is the second principal component of the data?
q-343711.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>{\lambda }_{3}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- the $3$rd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to the $3$rd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}.$

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned}
$$

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that:

- $\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ$ is a diagonal $3\times 3$ matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix $C$, and

- $V$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$

Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data.
So, the second principal component is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

U=[12−121212],V=[−132−1223432013−1321223] Consider the matrices U and V above. Let X be a 2×3 standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that X=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of X, what is the second principal component of the data?

a
 [−12012]
b
 [231323]
c
 [−1212]
d
 [−132432−132]
e
 [1212]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>λ3

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector v1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector v2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • the 3rd principal component is the unit eigenvector v3 corresponding to the 3rd eigenvalue λ3.

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to X is

C=1n−1XTX=1n−1(UΣVT)T(UΣVT)=1n−1VΣT(UTU)ΣVT=V(1n−1ΣTΣ)VT,

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix C. Notice that:

  • 1n−1ΣTΣ is a diagonal 3×3 matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix C, and

  • V is a 3×3 matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C.

Therefore, the columns of V are the principal components of the data. So, the second principal component is [−12012].

q-345598.name: Question 6
q-345598.problem:
A water pollution researcher measured $4$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4},$ for each water sample in a region with suspicions of water pollution. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular sample.
The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=9,\,{\sigma }_{2}=3,\,{\sigma }_{3}=2,\,{\sigma }_{4}=1.
$$

The researcher then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{1},$ where ${V}_{1}$ is the $4\times 1$ matrix consisting of the first principal component of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$
q-345598.worked_solution:
Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{4}$ are uncorrelated),

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},{y}_{4}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},{\sigma }_{3}^{2},{\sigma }_{4}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},{y}_{4}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(9)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(1)^{2} \\  & =95\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  researcher used only the first principal component, the remaining variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(9)^{2} \\  & =81.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{81}{95} \\  & ≈0.853 \\  & =85.3%.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

A water pollution researcher measured 4 particular features, x1,x2,x3,x4, for each water sample in a region with suspicions of water pollution. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix X, where each row contains measurements for a particular sample. The singular values of X are σ1=9,σ2=3,σ3=2,σ4=1. The researcher then converted the original observation matrix X into a new matrix Y using the equation Y=XV1, where V1 is the 4×1 matrix consisting of the first principal component of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix Y compared to the initial observation matrix X?

a
83.5%
b
85.3%
c
84.7%
d
89.5%
e
87.4%
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let V be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

Y=XV

we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1,y2,…,y4 are uncorrelated),

  • the features y1,y2,y3,y4 are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

  • the squares of the singular values σ12,σ22,σ32,σ42 represent the variances in the respective features y1,y2,y3,y4.

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

Total∝∑i=14σi2=(9)2+(3)2+(2)2+(1)2=95

Since the researcher used only the first principal component, the remaining variance is

Remaining∝∑i=11σi2=(9)2=81.

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

RemainingTotal=8195≈0.853=85.3%.

q-345600.name: Question 7
q-345600.problem:
A quality inspector measured $5$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{5},$ for each machine in a factory. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular machine.
The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=6,\,{\sigma }_{2}=4,\,{\sigma }_{3}=2,\,{\sigma }_{4}=1,\,{\sigma }_{5}=0.5.
$$

The inspector then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{2},$ where ${V}_{2}$ is the $5\times 2$ matrix consisting of the first two principal components of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$

Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},…,{\sigma }_{5}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{52}{57.25} \\  & ≈0.908 \\  & =90.8%.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

A scientist measured 5 particular features, x1,x2,…,x5, for each specimen among a group of animals in danger of extinction. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix X, where each row contains measurements for a particular specimen. The singular values of X are σ1=7,σ2=2,σ3=1,σ4=0.6,σ5=0.4. The scientist then converted the original observation matrix X into a new matrix Y using the equation Y=XV1, where V1 is the 5×1 matrix consisting of the first principal component of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix Y compared to the initial observation matrix X?

a
 91.8%
b
 83.5%
c
 89.9%
d
 92.4%
e
 86.5%
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let V be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

Y=XV

we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1,y2,…,y5 are uncorrelated),

  • the features y1,y2,…,y5 are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

  • the squares of the singular values σ12,σ22,…,σ52 represent the variances in the respective features y1,y2,…,y5.

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

Total∝∑i=15σi2=(7)2+(2)2+(1)2+(0.6)2+(0.4)2=54.52

Since the scientist used only the first principal component, the remaining variance is

Remaining∝∑i=11σi2=(7)2=49.

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

RemainingTotal=4954.52≈0.899=89.9%.

q-345605.name: Question 10
q-345605.problem:
A nutritionist measured $5$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{5},$ for each client in a group under a specific diet. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular client.
The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=6,\,{\sigma }_{2}=3,\,{\sigma }_{3}=2,\,{\sigma }_{4}=1,\,{\sigma }_{5}=0.6.
$$

The nutritionist then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{2},$ where ${V}_{2}$ is the $5\times 2$ matrix consisting of the first two principal components of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$
q-345605.worked_solution:
Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are uncorrelated),

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},…,{\sigma }_{5}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(6)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(0.6)^{2} \\  & =50.36\end{aligned}
$$

Since the nutritionist used only the first two principal components, the remaining variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(6)^{2}+(3)^{2} \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{45}{50.36} \\  & ≈0.894 \\  & =89.4%.\end{aligned}
$$
